f: Finance and procurement professionals value peer communities during digital transformation implementation because they provide essential support through the difficult transition period before digital tools deliver results. Professionals without community support expressed regret about not having a group of people to talk to and industry peers who had already gone through the process. These communities enable discussions about process change, change management, and change fatigue, allowing professionals to understand how other companies navigated the challenging hump where implementation is harder before it gets better. Having peers who are experiencing similar challenges helps professionals stay calm and manage the process effectively during this demanding phase.

Beyond immediate implementation support, peer communities help finance and procurement professionals build lasting networks and develop as thought leaders in their organizations. Members can pick up the phone and ask peers how they solved specific problems, discuss tax issues, and learn from real-life experiences of companies at different stages of transformation. The community also supports professionals in becoming digital leaders who can communicate data-driven insights back to leadership, measure impact, and change team mindsets post-automation. By bringing together people, process, and technology perspectives, these communities provide an ongoing support system that answers questions not just during implementation, but in the weeks, months, and years that follow.

f: Leaders managing digital transformation projects struggle with converting data and reporting into actionable change. While organizations now have access to extensive data and information about their teams and processes, they lack the capability to translate this into tangible impact, communicate results back to leadership, and measure outcomes effectively. This gap represents a critical missing piece as leaders navigate the complexity of modern transformation initiatives.

Beyond data utilization, leaders need support in managing team mindsets after automation is implemented. A significant challenge involves distinguishing between actionable metrics and benchmarked data that may not be relevant to their specific business context. For example, in procurement processes, one manufacturer might operate at 80% purchase order automation while another runs at 40%, making industry benchmarks meaningless for comparison. Leaders also struggle with understanding what comes next after achieving automation, requiring guidance on change management, process optimization, and team upskilling to identify new opportunities within their organizations.
